o: Dorsal column of the spinal cord
qs.e: Dysdiadochokinesia and past-pointing are classic signs of ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere pathology.

qs.q: During a neurological examination, a patient shows impaired tactile localization and stereognosis despite intact primary somatosensory cortex. Which cortical area is likely damaged?
o: Primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus.
Posterior parietal association cortex of the parietal lobe.
Prefrontal association cortex responsible for executive functions.
Primary visual cortex located in the calcarine sulcus.
Inferior temporal cortex involved in facial recognition.
qs.e: Association areas in the posterior parietal cortex integrate sensory inputs to enable complex tasks like stereognosis and spatial awareness.

qs.q: A 22-year-old male sustains a stab wound to the thoracic spine resulting in hemisection of the spinal cord. On neurological examination, which finding is expected on the ipsilateral side below the lesion?
o: Loss of light touch only with preserved motor power
Loss of motor function and conscious proprioception
Loss of pain and temperature sensation on this side
Flaccid paralysis with areflexia present indefinitely
qs.e: Brown-Séquard syndrome involves ipsilateral loss of motor function and proprioception due to involvement of the corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns. Pain and temperature loss occurs contralaterally because the spinothalamic tracts cross shortly after entry.

qs.q: A patient is able to flex and radially deviate the wrist during a neurological examination. Which muscle is primarily responsible for both of these specific actions?
qs.e: Flexor carpi radialis flexes the wrist and abducts (radially deviates) the wrist, inserting on the base of the second and third metacarpals. Flexor carpi ulnaris flexes and adducts (ulnarly deviates) the wrist.

qs.q: A patient presents with tongue deviation to the left side upon protrusion during a neurological examination. This physical finding indicates an injury to which of the following nerves?
qs.e: Hypoglossal nerve injury causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side due to unopposed contralateral muscle action. The other listed nerves do not control this specific motor deviation.

qs.q: During a neurological examination, a patient shows a characteristic 'claw hand' deformity resulting from a specific nerve injury. What is the underlying basis of this clinical presentation?
qs.e: Claw hand is the clinical effect of an ulnar nerve injury affecting the intrinsic hand muscles. Radial nerve injury typically presents as wrist drop rather than a claw hand.

ai.title: Paediatric Neurological Examination
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: The paediatric neurological examination is a structured assessment to localise neurological lesions, grade severity, and guide management in children. It requires adaptation for age and developmental stage. Prioritise ABCDE and urgent help if the child is acutely deteriorating or unconscious.

sections.p: The paediatric neurological examination is a systematic clinical process designed to evaluate the integrity and function of the central and peripheral nervous systems in children. It involves eliciting symptom chronology, associated systemic features, and risk factors, followed by a step-by-step examination to localise lesions, grade severity, and guide investigations and treatment. It is crucial to adapt the examination technique to the child's age, developmental stage, and level of cooperation.
b: Always assess ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) and call for urgent help if the child is unconscious or acutely deteriorating before a full neurological examination.
AVPU (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) is a rapid screening tool for consciousness, but not a replacement for the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) or a full neurological examination.
The examination aims to identify focal neurological signs, assess gait, tone, and abnormal movements, and evaluate developmental milestones.

sections.p: The presentation of neurological issues in children varies widely with age and the underlying condition. Infants may present with irritability, poor feeding, abnormal head growth, or developmental delay. Older children might complain of headaches, seizures, weakness, or changes in school performance. Clinicians must be vigilant for subtle signs.
b: History taking is paramount, focusing on prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal events, developmental milestones, seizure history, recent illnesses, and exposure to toxins.
Observation of the child's spontaneous activity, interaction, and play provides valuable initial information.
General examination includes vital signs, hydration status, nutrition, and assessment for dysmorphic features or cutaneous stigmata of neurocutaneous syndromes.

t.b: Answers: Is the child alert and responsive? What is their current neurological state? — GCS provides a more detailed, objective measure for older children; AVPU is a quick screen for all ages. A decreasing GCS score indicates neurological deterioration.

Answers: Are there focal deficits in facial movement, eye movement, or sensation? — Abnormalities can localise lesions to the brainstem or specific cranial nerve pathways. For example, a squint (CN III, IV, VI) or facial asymmetry (CN VII).

Answers: Is there weakness, spasticity, or hypotonia? Are reflexes brisk or absent? — Abnormalities help localise lesions to upper motor neuron (UMN), lower motor neuron (LMN), or muscle. For example, hypertonia and hyperreflexia suggest UMN lesion.

Answers: Is sensation intact? Are there areas of numbness or altered sensation? — Difficult to assess reliably in very young children, but crucial for localising spinal cord or peripheral nerve lesions in cooperative children.
Answers: Is there ataxia, dysmetria, or nystagmus? — Impairment suggests cerebellar dysfunction, affecting balance and coordinated movements. Observe gait for broad-based or unsteady patterns.
Answers: Is there evidence of leptomeningeal inflammation? — Positive signs (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's) indicate meningeal irritation, commonly seen in meningitis.

Answers: Is the child meeting age-appropriate milestones in motor, language, social, and cognitive domains? — Delays can indicate global developmental delay, specific neurological disorders, or environmental factors. Use age-appropriate screening tools.

sections.p: Investigations are guided by the clinical findings and suspected diagnosis. In low-resource settings, clinical acumen and basic laboratory tests are often the first line. Advanced imaging may be limited.

t.b: Answers: Are there systemic causes for neurological symptoms (e.g., anaemia, electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycaemia)? — Abnormalities can point to metabolic encephalopathy, infection, or systemic illness affecting the brain. If unavailable, clinical assessment of hydration and nutrition is key.

Answers: Is there meningitis, encephalitis, or subarachnoid haemorrhage? — Elevated white cells, low glucose, or high protein in CSF suggest infection (bacterial, viral, TB) or inflammation. Crucial for diagnosing meningitis, even if imaging is unavailable.

Answers: Is there cerebral malaria? — Positive smear for Plasmodium falciparum in an endemic area with neurological symptoms confirms cerebral malaria. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can also be used if microscopy is unavailable.

Answers: Is there HIV-associated encephalopathy or opportunistic infections? — Positive test indicates HIV infection, which can cause direct neurological complications or increase susceptibility to others (e.g., TB meningitis). Consider in any child with unexplained neurological symptoms in endemic areas.

Answers: Is there a structural lesion (e.g., tumour, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, abscess)? — Identifies gross structural abnormalities. Often limited availability; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal deficits to guide management.

Answers: Provides detailed imaging of brain structures, white matter, and subtle lesions. — Superior to CT for many conditions (e.g., demyelination, small tumours, posterior fossa lesions). Very limited availability in low-resource settings; clinical follow-up is critical.

Answers: Is there seizure activity or an epileptic syndrome? — Records brain electrical activity to identify epileptiform discharges. Limited availability; diagnosis often relies on clinical history of seizures.

sections.p: Recognising red flags is critical for timely intervention and preventing severe complications. These signs indicate acute neurological deterioration or potentially life-threatening conditions.
b: Rapidly deteriorating level of consciousness (decreasing GCS or AVPU).
New onset or worsening focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsy).
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: persistent vomiting, severe headache, papilloedema (if fundoscopy possible), Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration).
Status epilepticus (continuous seizure for 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness between them).
Meningeal signs (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's, Brudzinski's) in a febrile child.
Sudden onset of severe headache, especially with neck stiffness or altered mental status.
Acute ataxia or loss of balance.

sections.p: Follow-up is essential to monitor neurological recovery, manage chronic conditions, and address developmental needs. Prevention focuses on addressing underlying causes and promoting healthy development.
b: Regular developmental assessments to monitor progress and identify new delays or regression.
Physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy referrals for children with motor, fine motor, or communication deficits.
Nutritional support and management of comorbidities (e.g., epilepsy, cerebral palsy).
Immunisation programs to prevent infectious causes of neurological disease (e.g., measles, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcus).
Early identification and management of risk factors like malnutrition, anaemia, and exposure to neurotoxins.

sections.p: Several factors can lead to misleading findings during a paediatric neurological examination, especially in challenging clinical environments. Awareness of these pitfalls is crucial for accurate interpretation.
b: Uncooperative or distressed child: Crying, fear, or pain can make it difficult to assess tone, reflexes, and cranial nerves accurately. Repeated attempts or examining during sleep may be necessary.
Sedation or medication effects: Drugs can alter consciousness, tone, and reflexes, masking underlying neurological signs or creating new ones.
Developmental stage: Normal findings in an infant (e.g., primitive reflexes) are abnormal in an older child. Lack of age-appropriate knowledge can lead to misinterpretation.
Systemic illness: Severe dehydration, sepsis, or metabolic derangements can cause global neurological dysfunction (e.g., lethargy, hypotonia) that mimics primary neurological disease.
Limited equipment: Absence of ophthalmoscope for fundoscopy means papilloedema cannot be directly visualised, relying on other signs of raised ICP.
Cultural factors: Parental interpretation of symptoms or reluctance to disclose certain information can impact history taking.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset or worsening focal weakness or paralysis
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (e.g., persistent vomiting, severe headache, bulging fontanelle in infants)
Acute onset of severe headache with neck stiffness or fever
Sudden loss of vision or speech
Acute ataxia or inability to walk

faq.q: How do I adapt the neurological exam for an infant?
faq.a: Observe spontaneous movements, feeding, and interaction. Assess primitive reflexes (e.g., Moro, grasp, rooting), head circumference, and fontanelles. Cranial nerves are assessed through observation (e.g., tracking, facial symmetry during crying).

faq.q: What is the most important part of the paediatric neurological examination?
faq.a: The history, combined with careful observation of the child's spontaneous activity and interaction, often provides the most crucial diagnostic clues, especially in uncooperative children. Always assess ABCDE first in emergencies.

faq.q: What if I suspect meningitis but cannot do a lumbar puncture?
faq.a: If LP is contraindicated or unavailable, treat empirically for meningitis based on clinical suspicion (fever, meningeal signs, altered consciousness) with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Monitor closely for deterioration.
